drills.q: State the Raft quorum formula and compute it for N=3, N=4, and N=5. Why is N=4 wasteful?
drills.a: Quorum = floor(N/2)+1. N=3 -> 2 (tolerates 1 failure). N=4 -> 3 (tolerates 1 failure -- same as N=3). N=5 -> 3 (tolerates 2 failures). N=4 costs an extra node and vote for zero additional fault tolerance over N=3, which is why production clusters use odd sizes.

drills.q: Why is Raft's election timeout randomized instead of fixed?
drills.a: A fixed timeout means every follower times out at the same instant, causing a split vote every time (no candidate gets a majority). Randomizing from a range like 150-300ms means one node almost always fires first and wins before others become candidates.

drills.q: What is a Raft "term" used for, and what happens when a node receives a message with a lower term than its own?
drills.a: Term is a logical clock over leadership epochs, incremented on every election. A node rejects any RPC carrying a lower term than its own -- this is what lets everyone safely ignore a stale, isolated leader's heartbeats once the rest of the cluster has moved to a higher term.

drills.q: Distinguish "replicated" from "committed" in a Raft log, and explain why the distinction matters for when a client gets acked.
drills.a: Replicated means appended to some follower's log, possibly a minority. Committed means replicated to a majority. A client should only be acked after commit, because only majority-replication guarantees the entry survives any future leader election (via the election restriction).

drills.q: Explain the Raft election restriction and the safety property it guarantees.
drills.a: A candidate can win a vote only if its log is at least as up-to-date (by last-entry term, then length) as the voter's own log. This guarantees any future leader's log is a superset of all previously committed entries, so committed data can never be silently lost across a leader change.

drills.q: Raft vs Paxos: did Raft win because it's more powerful? Justify with evidence.
drills.a: No -- they are proven equivalent in the conditions under which they can make progress (both require a live majority). Raft won on comprehensibility: the 2014 user study of 43 students found most scored better on Raft comprehension questions than Paxos after learning both, because Raft decomposes the problem into independently explainable subproblems (election, replication, safety).

drills.q: What is a fencing token, and why does it have to be checked at the storage layer rather than the lock service?
drills.a: A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued on every lease/leadership acquisition. It has to be checked where the actual state-changing write happens because the lock service has no way to intercept a stale, paused client's write after it wakes up -- only the storage layer sees that write and can reject it if its token is lower than the last one seen.

drills.q: A Lamport timestamp of event A is less than event B's timestamp. What, precisely, can you conclude?
drills.a: Almost nothing about their causal relationship. If A causally precedes B, C(A) < C(B) is guaranteed, but the converse doesn't hold -- two fully unrelated, concurrent events can end up with any relative ordering due to arbitrary tie-breaking. Lamport clocks give a total order, not a causality guarantee.

drills.q: Why do vector clocks not scale in high-churn distributed systems, concretely?
drills.a: A vector clock carries one integer per participating node (O(n) space), and n grows with every node or client that has ever contributed to that data's history and doesn't shrink without active pruning. In high-churn systems this becomes real, growing bandwidth and storage overhead per stored version.

drills.q: Explain how a Hybrid Logical Clock computes its next value, and why it avoids the vector clock's scaling problem while still giving causal ordering.
drills.a: HLC keeps (physical_time, logical_counter). If current wall-clock time exceeds the max of last-seen HLC values (own and received), adopt it and reset the counter to 0; otherwise keep the higher physical component and increment the counter to break ties. This gives causal ordering like Lamport clocks, but at O(1) space per event since it's a single pair, not one entry per node -- no vector clock-style per-participant blowup.

drills.q: A candidate claims "we use Raft so we're split-brain proof." Where is this wrong, with a concrete example?
drills.a: Raft's split-brain prevention holds only for the log it manages -- it prevents two leaders from both committing entries in the same term. It says nothing about side effects a stale leader triggers OUTSIDE the log, e.g. a scheduler that calls an external email API on every tick: that call isn't gated by commit-index checks, only by in-memory leader state, which can be stale for as long as the partition lasts before heartbeat timeout forces a step-down.

drills.q: Design lease-based leader election for a job scheduler needing exactly one active scheduler. What is the failure mode if you skip fencing tokens, and what specifically triggers it?
drills.a: Without fencing tokens, a scheduler process that experiences a GC pause or OS preemption longer than the lease TTL keeps believing it's leader when it wakes up, because it has no way to know time passed while paused. It can then dispatch a job concurrently with the new leader (which acquired the lease after the old one's expired), producing a duplicate execution -- the fix is a monotonically increasing fencing token on every acquisition, checked by whatever system executes the scheduled jobs.
